newsitem.title: USA: Clinton downplays fear stock drop would hit economy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton downplays fear stock drop would hit economy.

text.p: President Clinton Friday played down fears that a sudden drop in the stock market would hurt the economy and pointed out that the long-term trend in stock prices is up.

"Over the long term, if we have the discipline -- all of us -- to ride out the inevitable changes in the markets, the markets have produced a very steady growth," Clinton told a news conference unveiling his new economic team.
That has been the case even when the market has crashed, as happened back in 1929 and in 1987, he added.

After rising to record levels last month, stock prices have dipped recently as investors grew concerned about current prices. While some have said stocks were overvalued and could crash again, other analysts have noted that conditions now are different from before the '29 and '87 crashes.

Clinton said he was "very pleased" that many Americans have made a lot of money investing in the stock market. "I'm proud of the vibrant markets we have," he said. "They will change, they go up and down, they always do.
"My job is to keep the underlying fundamentals sound" so that any stock price drops do not end up damaging the economy, he said.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan rattled global markets last week after he said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects asset prices because that could end up doing damage to the economy.
Clinton declined to comment on Greenspan's remarks.

But he flatly rejected suggestions that a stock market drop would inevitably lead to an economic tailspin, pointing in particular to the economy's ability to weather the October 1987 stock market crash.

On Black Monday, Oct. 19, 1987, the Dow Jones industrial avarge fell 508 points, or 22.6 percent. But the economy continued to expand, thanks in part to interest rate cuts by the Fed, the nation's central bank.
The 30-share Dow index dipped modestly Friday after Clinton's remarks but managed to close up 1.16 points at 6,304.87. The rise followed two days of losses totalling 170 points.
Some analysts said that Clinton, like Greenspan, may have been trying to inject some sobriety into financial markets.

"I think Greenspan has decided jawboning is better than using monetary policy and it looks like Clinton has decided to pick up on that," Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Wall Street broker Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"I don't think Clinton has the same credibility," Cripps added. "People will view it as a political statement."
Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd., said Clinton's comments did not have much effect on the market.

"The market is extremely, extremely volatile. When he said he was not concerned about the stock market and doesn't think a drop would hurt the economy he was being coached. Politicians shouldn't talk about the stock market."
